podcast.title: Peele Session with David Bowie (May 23rd, 1972)
podcast.body: The Spiders from Mars, as David Bowie's band, participated in a "Peele Session" on May 23rd, 1972. These sessions, overseen by DJ John Peel at the BBC, were a significant platform for artists to perform and record live, especially during periods of "Needle Time" restrictions. "Here's something from May 23rd, 1972, when an artist on the asset named David Bowie dropped in for a session with his band, The Spiders from Mars."

podcast.title: Top of the Pops Performance (July 6, 1972)
podcast.body: The Spiders from Mars performed with David Bowie on Top of the Pops on July 6, 1972. Guitarist Mick Ronson was dressed in a gold one-piece, and shared a moment of public affection with Bowie (Bowie draped his arm around Ronson's shoulders) that was highly shocking for the era. "Onstage with him was his guitarist, Mick Ronson, dressed in a gold one piece."

xref.title: Sexual Identity Declaration (1972)
xref.body: Six months before the release of *The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders from Mars*, David Bowie declared himself to be gay. Given that homosexuality had only been decriminalized in England in 1967, this public confession from a major pop star had a huge liberating effect on individuals afraid to reveal their own sexual orientation. "Six months before the album came, a Bowie declared himself to be gay."

xref.title: Top of the Pops Performance (July 6, 1972)
xref.body: Bowie's seminal performance on Top of the Pops on July 6, 1972, with The Spiders from Mars, was highly influential. Dressed in a quilted jumpsuit, red boxing boots with green laces, and bright red-orange hair, Bowie's anisocoria (permanently dilated pupil from a childhood fight) added to his "otherworldly look." His public display of affection towards guitarist Mick Ronson (draping his arm around his shoulders) was considered "super duper gay" for the era and had a profound impact, leading to the immediate appearance of "Ziggy Clones" and helping young people feel accepted in their sexuality. "One especially interesting performance was on top of the pops on the BBC, July 6th, 1972."

xref.title: Equipment Theft by Steve Jones (July 1973)
xref.body: During a multi-night stand at the Hammersmith Odeon in London in July 1973, David Bowie and The Spiders from Mars had microphones and amplifiers stolen by a young thief named Steve Jones, who later became the guitarist for the Sex Pistols. It is speculated that this stolen gear was used by the Sex Pistols in their early rehearsals and gigs in 1975, contributing to the punk rock era. "When Bowie and the spiders from Mars loaded into the Hammersmith Odien in London in July 1973 for a multi-night stand, a young thief named Steve Jones broke into the theatre and made off with a bunch of microphones and amplifiers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Theft of Bowie's Gear (July 1973)
xref.body: As a young thief in July 1973, Steve Jones broke into the Hammersmith Odeon during a David Bowie and The Spiders from Mars' engagement and stole microphones and amplifiers. This gear is believed to have been used by Jones and the Sex Pistols in their early rehearsals and gigs starting in 1975, initiating their contribution to the punk rock era. "a young thief named Steve Jones broke into the theatre and made off with a bunch of microphones and amplifiers."

xref.title: Blackstar Release on 69th Birthday (January 8, 2016)
xref.body: Bowie's final album, "Blackstar," was released on Friday, January 8, 2016, coinciding with his 69th birthday. That same night, Holy Holy, a band featuring some of his former Spiders from Mars backing musicians, played a show in New York City, and while there was speculation Bowie might appear, he did not; instead, the band left him a voicemail with the crowd singing "Happy Birthday." "On Friday, January 18, the day Blackstar, that album he'd been working on during his illness, was released, and it was also Bowie's 69th birthday."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "K. West" Sign
xref.body: The famous "K. West" sign, under which David Bowie posed for the *Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars* album cover on Heddon Street in London, was from a fur store. This sign has become a central piece of the conspiracy theory claiming Bowie predicted Kanye West's rise. It was later purchased by an anonymous collector with alleged music industry connections. "Forget that k West was a store that sold furs. It does matter, but if you sound the k West, you also get quest."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with David Bowie
xref.body: As David Bowie's Spiders From Mars guitarist, Mick Ronson collaborated with Bowie to produce Lou Reed's 1972 album, *Transformer*. Their work helped Reed find a new sound, demonstrating Ronson's influence beyond his guitar playing. "Bowie and his spiders from Mars guitarist, Mick Ronson, helped Lou find a new sound."

xref.title: Inspiration for Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: Iggy Pop, a friend of David Bowie, was one of the two people who inspired the name for Bowie's alien rock star character, Ziggy, in *The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders from Mars*. "And that name was inspired by two people, Bowie's new friend Iggy Pop, and a Texas proto-psychobilly singer named Norman O'Dan, who went by the handle of the legendary Stardust Cowboy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: Norman O'Dan, a Texas proto-psychobilly singer also known as The Legendary Stardust Cowboy, was a big fan of space travel and admired by David Bowie. He was one of the two people who inspired the name for Bowie's alien rock star character, Ziggy, in *The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders from Mars*. "And that name was inspired by two people, Bowie's new friend Iggy Pop, and a Texas proto-psychobilly singer named Norman O'Dan, who went by the handle of the legendary Stardust Cowboy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Kanye West Prediction Theory
xref.body: A conspiracy theory claims David Bowie predicted the rise of Kanye West back in 1972. Proponents cite Bowie's *Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars* album (released June 16, 1972) and its song "Five Years" as foretelling the event, noting Kanye's birth on June 8, 1977, almost five years later. The theory also highlights the "K. West" sign visible on the *Ziggy Stardust* album cover (from a fur store), interpreting it as a direct reference, and Bowie's final album, *Black Star*, as an "anointment" of Kanye, referred to as a "Black Star." Bowie's known visionary capabilities regarding digital music, social media, and gender fluidity are used to support his ability to predict Kanye's ascendance. "Did David Bowie predict the rise of Kanye West way back in 1972?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Origin of Ziggy Stardust's Haircut
xref.body: A popular narrative recounts that during the "Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars" album sessions, Bowie expressed a desire for a different look, telling his wife Angie, "I want to cut my hair and I want to look different," and suggested dyeing it red. "One version of the story says that during the sessions for what would become the Ziggy Stardust and the spiders from Mars album, Bowie woke up one morning and said to Angie over his orange juice, I want to cut my hair and I want to look different."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Patronage of Lou Reed
xref.body: Bowie was also a great admirer of Lou Reed and The Velvet Underground, recognizing Reed's talent despite him being on the fringes and largely unknown. Bowie offered his patronage, leading him to produce Reed's 1972 album *Transformer*, collaborating with his Spiders From Mars guitarist, Mick Ronson, to help Reed find a new sound. "Bowie did, though, and he offered to lend his patronage to Lou."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Toronto Concert After Death
xref.body: After Bowie's death, a planned concert in Toronto with the surviving members of his Spiders from Mars band proceeded. The mood at this show was described as "stunned," with plenty of denial evident among fans as the truth of his passing began to sink in. "I was at that Tuesday show in Toronto, and the word to describe the mood was stunned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ziggy Stardust Persona
xref.body: Bowie immersed himself fully into the persona of Ziggy Stardust, a "doomed pansexual alien." This character was a "pre-packaged synthetic ultra glamorous, ultra theatrical, fantastical rock star" that fundamentally changed the presentation of rock music. "Bowie immersed himself into this new persona, this doomed pansexual alien, and he invented a new name for himself. It was Ziggy Stardust."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ziggy Stardust Tour Theatricality
xref.body: The tour supporting "The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders from Mars" (January 29, 1972 - July 3, 1973) set a new standard for theatricality in rock, incorporating "big end themic songs, costume changes, choreography, makeup, tall boots, and ridiculously high platform shoes" along with "daring sexual ambiguity." "the tour, which ran from January 29th, 1972 to July 3rd, 1973, was the most theatrical thing that rock had ever seen to that point."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
